solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Feature of pretty close inspections (4,5)

blocks.note: "pretty" is the adjective standing for an attractive person; what marks them out is an attractive appearance
examining something carefully, a long hard stare at it

annotation.surface: It reads like a line about how attractive something looks when you examine it up close.
annotation.walkthrough: "Pretty close" wants to be one phrase meaning fairly near; the split falls after "pretty", which is the attractive person, not the adverb.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase has two senses: attractiveness, which is what makes someone pretty, and careful glances, which is what close inspections are.

entries.clue: Pass on advice to young man (2,4)

blocks.note: pass on is the euphemism for dying; the answer is an older slang phrase for the same thing
a famous nineteenth-century American slogan urging young men to seek their fortune on the frontier

annotation.surface: Someone is relaying a piece of advice to a youngster.
annotation.walkthrough: "Pass on" looks like handing advice along; it is the euphemism for dying. The second half quotes the slogan "Go west, young man".
annotation.definitionFit: Go west is First World War slang for being killed, and the same words complete the pioneer-era slogan the clue half-quotes.

entries.clue: Tennis star, really big, with alias (5)

blocks.note: OS = outsize, the clothing-label abbreviation for very large
aka = also known as, which introduces an alias

annotation.surface: A description of a huge tennis star who plays under another name.
annotation.walkthrough: Naomi Osaka is a Japanese tennis champion; the city of the same name is a decoy the definition steers away from.
annotation.definitionFit: Naomi Osaka has won several Grand Slam singles titles, a definition by example.

entries.clue: Those inclined to offer shares? (6,9)

blocks.note: the surface offers generous people, willing to do something; a ship that lists is inclined in the other sense, leaning over
not sharing out sweets but selling stock, which only businesses on an exchange can do

annotation.surface: People who are willing to share things with others.
annotation.walkthrough: "Inclined" reads as willing; the answer takes it literally, since leaning over is listing. The question mark flags that pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A listed company has its shares traded on a stock exchange, and listed also means tilted, so the clue fits both ways.

entries.clue: No overnight case (10)

blocks.note: the surface suggests travelling light; the real sense is not staying the night somewhere
not a suitcase but a medical case, someone being treated

annotation.surface: Travelling without an overnight bag.
annotation.walkthrough: "Overnight case" suggests luggage; "case" is the medical sense, a patient.
annotation.definitionFit: An outpatient is treated at a hospital without being admitted overnight.

entries.clue: Thus see unaided (4)

blocks.note: so = thus
lo = see!, as in "lo and behold"

annotation.surface: An instruction to look at something with the naked eye.
annotation.walkthrough: "See unaided" reads as naked-eye viewing, but "see" belongs to the wordplay and "unaided" stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a solo flight or effort is made without help.

entries.clue: Small jug that one shouldn’t drink from (5)

annotation.definition: Small jug that one shouldn’t drink from

blocks.note: S = small, as on a clothing label
a ewer is a large water jug

annotation.surface: A warning about a little jug that is not for drinking out of.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is just "Small jug"; the whole clue then describes the answer too, a channel of liquid you must never drink.
annotation.definitionFit: A sewer carries waste water, the last thing anyone should drink, and its name is a small letter plus a jug.

entries.clue: Money received by crook? (8,7)

blocks.note: an income, some payment coming in
the surface offers a criminal; in Australian and British slang crook also means unwell

annotation.surface: A criminal's takings.
annotation.walkthrough: "Crook" poses as a criminal but is the slang for ill. Sickness benefit was the UK state payment to people off work through illness.
annotation.definitionFit: Sickness benefit is money the state pays to someone too ill to work, which a crook person would receive.

entries.clue: Scratched and pinched (9)

blocks.note: the racing term for a horse pulled out of a race before it starts
a pinched face is thin and drawn, shrunken in on itself

annotation.surface: Someone has been clawed and nipped.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like minor injuries. "Scratched" means pulled from the field; "pinched" is a gaunt, shrunken look.
annotation.definitionFit: A scratched runner has been taken out of the race, and a pinched, retiring look is drawn inward, the two senses of the answer.

entries.clue: In studies, he’d crushed ginger nuts (8)

indicatorNotes.In: the crushed letters go in the word for studies
indicatorNotes.crushed: crushing breaks something up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: to read a subject at university is to study it
HED rearranged, placed inside READS after RE

annotation.surface: A person bashing up ginger nut biscuits between study sessions.
annotation.walkthrough: Ginger nuts are British biscuits, so the phrase reads as snack food; here "nuts" is slang for heads.
annotation.definitionFit: A "nut" is slang for a head, so ginger nuts are people with red hair.

entries.clue: Repartee about bowler’s thingy (7)

indicatorNotes.about: the wit goes round the other piece

blocks.note: repartee is quick wit
a bowler is a hat, and bowler's = bowler is, so HAT'S

annotation.surface: Banter about a cricket bowler's unnamed object.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bowler" suggests cricket; it is the hard round hat. The apostrophe-S reads as possessive but stands for "is".
annotation.definitionFit: Both are placeholder words for an object whose name escapes you.

entries.clue: Latin dictionary in which “felis” is found (7)

indicatorNotes.in which: the Latin word's meaning sits in the dictionary

blocks.note: L = Latin
OED = Oxford English Dictionary
felis is Latin for cat

annotation.surface: Looking up the Latin word felis in a dictionary.
annotation.walkthrough: "Latin dictionary" reads as one book; Latin is only an abbreviation, and the dictionary is an English one. The Latin word must be translated before it goes in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something found has been located.

entries.clue: One of keys A and B will open box (5,3)

indicatorNotes.will open: the new letters open up the box word and sit inside it

blocks.note: to spar is to box
the ace is the A in a pack of cards
B stays as itself, following ACE inside SPAR

annotation.surface: Keys labelled A and B are needed to unlock a box.
annotation.walkthrough: The keys look like padlock keys opening a box; they are keyboard keys, and "box" is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: The space bar is the long key at the bottom of a keyboard, a definition by example.

entries.clue: Wound up performing at the Fringe? (2,4)

blocks.note: wound up = tense, nervous
on = performing; a fringe is a border

annotation.surface: An anxious comedian doing a show at the Edinburgh Fringe.
annotation.walkthrough: The Edinburgh Fringe is the city's huge summer arts festival. The question mark warns that the second half is read literally.
annotation.definitionFit: Nervy and tense is one sense; the other takes the words literally, performing (on) at a border (edge).

entries.clue: Promise of union action (10)

blocks.note: the union is a marriage, and this is the promise to marry
military action, a battle

annotation.surface: A trade union's pledge to strike.
annotation.walkthrough: "Union action" reads as industrial action; the union is a marriage and the action is a fight.
annotation.definitionFit: The word covers both a betrothal and a clash between armed forces.

entries.clue: Devout cardinal isn’t bad for Christian settlement (8,6)

indicatorNotes.bad: bad letters are in the wrong order

blocks.note: pi = pious, devout
CARDINALISNT rearranged

annotation.surface: A religious remark about a pious cardinal and a Christian community.
annotation.walkthrough: "Christian" is Fletcher Christian, who led the Bounty mutineers to settle the island in 1790, not the faith the cardinal suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: Pitcairn Island was settled by Fletcher Christian and the Bounty mutineers, whose descendants still live there.

entries.clue: Largely popular officer (2,7)

blocks.note: in = fashionable, popular
a general is a senior army officer

annotation.surface: A well-liked officer, mostly.
annotation.walkthrough: "Largely" can look like a comment on the officer's size; it is an adverb meaning mostly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean for the most part.

entries.clue: We had to include gag — sorry (8)

indicatorNotes.to include: one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: we had = we'd
to gag is to retch

annotation.surface: An apology for a joke that had to go into a show.
annotation.walkthrough: "Gag" looks like a joke; it is the throat's heave. "Sorry" is not an apology but the adjective, as in a sorry sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Sorry in the sense of pitiful: a sorry state is a miserable, pitiable one.

entries.clue: Soldier and mad outlaw in communist military group (10,4)

indicatorNotes.in: the three pieces sit inside the communist

blocks.note: a red is a communist
GI = an American soldier
mental = mad, informally
to outlaw is to ban

annotation.surface: A deranged soldier and a bandit hiding in a communist army unit.
annotation.walkthrough: "Outlaw" poses as a bandit; it is the verb. "Military group" sounds like troops, but the group here plays music.
annotation.definitionFit: A regimental band is the musical group attached to an army regiment.

entries.clue: Firm support — it turns out the same (6)

blocks.note: Co. = company, a firm
a pier is a supporting pillar

annotation.surface: Steady backing that ends up unchanged.
annotation.walkthrough: "Turns out" means produces, as a machine turns out work, not "proves to be".
annotation.definitionFit: A copier churns out pages identical to the original, a cryptic description rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: Polynesian in trouble, not coming back (6)

indicatorNotes.coming back: the letters return the way they came, right to left

blocks.note: to nag is to trouble, to pester
not as itself

annotation.surface: A Pacific islander in difficulty, never returning.
annotation.walkthrough: "In trouble" looks like a phrase; "in" is only a link and "trouble" is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Tonga is a Polynesian kingdom in the South Pacific, so its people are Polynesians.

entries.clue: Age hidden by fat old painter (8)

indicatorNotes.hidden by: the age is covered by the fat, so sits inside it

blocks.note: an eon is an age
lard is pig fat
O = old

annotation.surface: An elderly overweight artist whose years are disguised by his bulk.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fat old painter" reads as one unkind description; "old" is only the letter on the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci is the Renaissance painter of the Mona Lisa, a definition by example.

entries.clue: Monarch playing party piece? (5)

blocks.note: R = rex or regina, king or queen
on = playing, performing
a do is a party

annotation.surface: A king doing his party piece.
annotation.walkthrough: "Party piece" is one phrase in the surface; "party" goes to the wordplay and "piece" alone is the musical composition.
annotation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical piece with a recurring main theme, a definition by example.

entries.clue: A winner, but no married bloke (4)

indicatorNotes.no: the married letter is taken away

blocks.note: a champ is a winner
M = married, removed from CHAMP

annotation.surface: A victorious man who is still single.
annotation.walkthrough: M for married is the genealogical abbreviation. Bloke is British slang for a man.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are informal British words for a man.

entries.clue: Not so easy to fit copper into grating (7)

indicatorNotes.to fit: fitting something in places it inside
indicatorNotes.into: names the word the copper goes inside

blocks.note: a grating voice is harsh
a copper is a policeman: DI = Detective Inspector

annotation.surface: Squeezing a piece of copper metal through a grate is tricky.
annotation.walkthrough: "Copper" and "grating" read as metalwork; one is a police officer and the other an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: The -ish ending softens hard to fairly hard, which is the understated not so easy.

entries.clue: Mr F Ward, Independent (7)

blocks.note: EF is the spelt-out name of the letter F
to ward off is to fend off
I = independent

annotation.surface: A name tag for an independent politician called F Ward.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is laid out like a ballot paper listing a candidate, so "Mr F Ward" looks like one name; "Mr" alone is the definition and "Ward" is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Effendi is a Turkish and Middle Eastern courtesy title for a man, used much as Mr is.

entries.clue: Valleys in feudal estates (5)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits inside the following words

blocks.note: the run starts after FEU and stops before TATES

annotation.surface: Valleys that were once parts of a lord's lands.
annotation.walkthrough: The dales, as in the Yorkshire Dales, are the valleys of northern England; the surface reaches for medieval landholding to hide them.
annotation.definitionFit: Dale is the northern English word for a valley.

entries.clue: Dainty little Parisian quartet (5,4)

blocks.note: the French word for little
a quartet is four

annotation.surface: Four refined little French musicians.
annotation.walkthrough: "Dainty" looks like an adjective but is the noun: a dainty is a small delicacy.
annotation.definitionFit: A petit four is a tiny fancy cake served after dinner, exactly the sort of delicacy called a dainty.
